subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 13 periods = 520 minutes
Total: 13 periods · 8h 40min

periods.activity_title: Floors Above and Below: Meeting Negative Numbers

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Activity 1, p.243
textbook_items_in_class.description: Students identify floors and their numbers in Bela's Building of Fun from a diagram, and determine what to press on the lift to travel four floors up and three floors down.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example (Addition to keep track of movement), p.245
textbook_items_in_class.description: Starting from Food Court (Floor +1), pressing +2 in the lift leads to target floor (+1)+(+2)=+3, illustrating the rule Starting Floor + Movement = Target Floor.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 10.1 p.245
textbook_items_in_class.description: Start from Floor +2 and press –3. Where do you reach? Write an expression.

time_bands.activity: Activity 1, p.243 ("students identify floors and their numbers in Bela's Building....") — students examine the building diagram together, naming each floor from –3 (Cinema) up to +4 (Ice Cream), reading the lift buttons, and articulating how positive and negative signs distinguish above-ground from below-ground floors.

Teacher walks through Example (Addition to keep track of movement), p.245 ("Starting from Food Court (Floor +1), pressing +2....") — writing the rule Starting Floor + Movement = Target Floor on the board, then inviting students to explain the sign of each floor number using the diagram before any symbol is written.

Students work individually on Figure it Out Q1, section 10.1 p.245 ("Start from Floor +2 and press –3. Where do you reach?....") — writing the full expression and circling the destination on their building sketch.
Pairs share their expressions aloud; teacher records varied phrasings on the board and draws out the pattern that moving down shrinks the floor number, reinforcing the meaning of a negative result.

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently confuse the sign of a floor number with the direction of movement — watch for children who write '–3 means press down 3' but then record the destination incorrectly when the starting floor is also negative. Ground every answer in the building diagram before moving to symbolic form. Example (Addition to keep track of movement), p.245 can be revisited as a self-study reference after class.

periods.activity_title: Combining Button Presses: Addition on the Number Line

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example (Combining button presses), p.245
textbook_items_in_class.description: Gurmit presses +2 by mistake then –3 to correct; result is (+2)+(–3)=–1, illustrating that combining button presses is addition.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example (Back to zero), p.246
textbook_items_in_class.description: Pressing +3 and then –3 returns to Floor 0; introduces the concept of additive inverse. (+3)+(–3)=0.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 10.1 p.245
textbook_items_in_class.description: Evaluate seven expressions (a–g) as Starting Floor + Movement: (+1)+(+4), (+4)+(+1), (+4)+(–3), (–1)+(+2), (–1)+(+1), 0+(+2), 0+(–2).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out, section 10.1 p.246
textbook_items_in_class.description: Evaluate four expressions (a–d) as combined button presses: (+1)+(+4), (+4)+(+1), (+4)+(–3)+(–2), (–1)+(+2)+(–3).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 10.1 p.245
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find multiple starting floors and the movements needed to reach Floor –5; write expressions of the form (starting)+(movement)=–5.

time_bands.activity: Teacher presents Example (Combining button presses), p.245 ("Gurmit presses +2 by mistake then –3 to correct....") and Example (Back to zero), p.246 ("Pressing +3 and then –3 returns to Floor 0....") — students narrate what happens at each button press before the symbolic form is written, discovering the additive inverse idea in their own words.

Students work through Figure it Out Q2, section 10.1 p.245 ("Evaluate seven expressions (a–g) as Starting Floor + Movement....") and Figure it Out, section 10.1 p.246 ("Evaluate four expressions (a–d) as combined button presses....") — each expression traced on a sketch of the building before writing a number sentence.

Figure it Out Q3, section 10.1 p.245 ("Find multiple starting floors and movements needed to reach Floor –5....") — students work in pairs to generate as many expressions as they can, then share with another pair to compare findings and notice patterns in the pairs that sum to –5.
Class discussion: teacher asks 'What do you notice about numbers that cancel each other out?' guiding students to articulate the Back-to-Zero (additive inverse) idea without yet naming it formally.

periods.teacher_notes: Having established that floor numbering uses positive and negative signs, this unit deepens the idea by treating multiple button presses as a single addition. A common error is reversing the sign of the movement when the starting floor is negative — for example writing (–1)+(+2) as going down instead of up. Use the building sketch throughout to verify every answer spatially before accepting a symbolic result.
materials: Building sketch from previous work or freshly drawn

periods.activity_title: Ordering Integers: Who Is Higher, Who Is Lower?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 10.1 p.247
textbook_items_in_class.description: Compare six pairs of integers using < or > by referring to the Building of Fun: –2 vs +5, –5 vs +4, –5 vs –3, +6 vs –6, 0 vs –4, 0 vs +4.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 10.1 p.247
textbook_items_in_class.description: Compare six pairs of larger integers with < or >: –10 vs –12, +17 vs –10, 0 vs –20, +9 vs –9, –25 vs –7, +15 vs –17.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 10.1 p.247
textbook_items_in_class.description: Given Floor A=–12, Floor D=–1, Floor E=+1 on a vertical number line, find the numbers of Floors B, C, F, G, and H.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 10.1 p.247
textbook_items_in_class.description: Mark four floors (–7, –4, +3, –10) on a vertical building diagram.

time_bands.activity: Teacher poses an opening question: 'If Floor –5 and Floor –3 are both underground, which one is lower?' — students respond with reasoning, then teacher connects their language to the idea that a more negative number is smaller, drawing a short vertical number line on the board.

Students complete Figure it Out Q1, section 10.1 p.247 ("Compare six pairs of integers using < or >....") and Figure it Out Q2, section 10.1 p.247 ("Compare six pairs of larger integers with < or >....") — recording their reasoning in a sentence alongside each inequality symbol.

Students work on Figure it Out Q3, section 10.1 p.247 ("Given Floor A=–12, Floor D=–1, Floor E=+1 on a vertical number line, find Floors B, C, F, G, H....") and Figure it Out Q4, section 10.1 p.247 ("Mark four floors on a vertical building diagram....") — using a hand-drawn vertical number line to position each floor before writing the number.

Students compare their vertical number lines in groups of three, resolve disagreements by pointing to which floor is physically lower in the building, and articulate the rule: 'further below zero means a smaller integer.'

periods.teacher_notes: Having added and subtracted on the building, students now formalise ordering. The most common error here is treating –25 as greater than –7 because 25 > 7 in isolation — consistently returning to 'which floor is lower in the building?' disrupts this. Figure it Out Q3 and Q4 on p.247 are excellent for homework if time is short.
materials: Ruler for drawing vertical number lines

periods.activity_title: Subtraction as a Journey: Finding the Movement Needed

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example (Subtraction a), p.249
textbook_items_in_class.description: Target Floor –1, Starting Floor –2: movement needed is (+1). Expression: (–1)–(–2)=(+1).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example (Subtraction b), p.249
textbook_items_in_class.description: Target Floor –1, Starting Floor +3: movement needed is –4. Expression: (–1)–(+3)=(–4).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example (Subtraction c), p.249
textbook_items_in_class.description: Target Floor +2, Starting Floor –2: movement needed is +4. Expression: (+2)–(–2)=(+4).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out, section 10.1 p.249
textbook_items_in_class.description: Complete ten subtraction expressions (a–j) as movement from Starting Floor to Target Floor: (+1)–(+4), 0–(+2), (+4)–(+1), 0–(–2), (+4)–(–3), (–4)–(–3), (–1)–(+2), (–2)–(–2), (–1)–(+1), (+3)–(–3).

time_bands.activity: Teacher presents Example (Subtraction a), p.249 ("Target Floor –1, Starting Floor –2: movement needed is +1...."), Example (Subtraction b), p.249 ("Target Floor –1, Starting Floor +3: movement needed is –4...."), and Example (Subtraction c), p.249 ("Target Floor +2, Starting Floor –2: movement needed is +4....") — for each, students first guess the movement by pointing on a vertical number line, then verify by checking Starting + Movement = Target.

Students work through Figure it Out, section 10.1 p.249 ("Complete ten subtraction expressions as movement from Starting Floor to Target Floor....") — each expression set up as 'I am at ___, I want to get to ___; what do I press?' with answers verified by adding movement back to starting floor.
Students pair up and pose three original subtraction problems to each other using floor numbers of their own choice, then solve each other's problems and check by addition.

Teacher highlights the result of example (c): (+2)–(–2)=+4, asking 'What do you notice about subtracting a negative?' and collecting student observations to anchor the pattern that will reappear in larger contexts.

periods.teacher_notes: Having ordered integers on the vertical line, this unit reframes subtraction as 'what movement takes me from the starting floor to the target floor?' — a shift that prevents the common error of treating subtraction as always making a number smaller. Watch for students who evaluate (+2)–(–2) as 0 by ignoring the sign of the number being subtracted; the verification step (Starting + Movement = Target) catches this immediately.
materials: Vertical number line drawn on paper or board

periods.activity_title: Larger Integers, the Number Line, and Converting Subtraction

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example (Adding larger numbers, mine), p.250
Example (Infinite lift subtraction), p.251
textbook_items_in_class.description: Computing +2000–(–200): going from –200 to +2000 on the infinite lift requires pressing +2200. Reveals that subtracting a negative equals adding a positive.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example (Conversion subtraction to addition), p.255
textbook_items_in_class.description: Breaking journey from 2 to –3: (a) 2→0 is –2, (b) 0→–3 is –3; total movement is –3+(–2)=–5. Shows –3–2=–5 with no subtraction in second form.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out, section 10.1 p.251
textbook_items_in_class.description: Complete seven expressions using the mine/larger number context (a–g): (+40)+__=+200, (+40)+__=–200, (–50)+__=+200, (–50)+__=–200, (–200)–(–40), (+200)–(+40), (–200)–(+40). Verify using the mineshaft.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out, section 10.1 p.251
Figure it Out, section 10.1 p.255
textbook_items_in_class.description: Use unmarked number lines to evaluate four expressions: –125+(–30), +105–(–55), +80–(–150), –99–(–200).

time_bands.activity: Teacher presents Example (Adding larger numbers, mine), p.250 ("Mine context: (+40)+(+60)=+100 and (–90)+(–55)=–145....") and Example (Infinite lift subtraction), p.251 ("Computing +2000–(–200): going from –200 to +2000 requires pressing +2200....") — connecting the mine's vertical scale to the building context already familiar, then drawing the key conclusion on the board: subtracting a negative equals adding a positive.

Students complete Figure it Out, section 10.1 p.251 ("Complete seven expressions using the mine/larger number context....") — each blank filled by imagining the lift journey and verifying via the inverse addition.

Teacher introduces Example (Conversion subtraction to addition), p.255 ("Breaking journey from 2 to –3: 2→0 is –2, 0→–3 is –3....") — students then apply the conversion rule to Figure it Out, section 10.1 p.251 ("Evaluate eight expressions by imagining a suitable lift....") for selected items.

Students sketch unmarked number lines for Figure it Out, section 10.1 p.255 ("Use unmarked number lines to evaluate four expressions....") — marking only the starting point, the movement arrow, and the landing point, then recording the result.

periods.teacher_notes: Having established subtraction as movement between floors, this unit extends the same logic to large integers and then to the unmarked number line. The key conceptual milestone is the equivalence (+40)–(–50) = (+40)+(+50): students who reach this naturally from the mine context rarely confuse it later. Watch for students who draw the number line backwards (larger numbers on the left) — correct this with a quick gesture to the building's vertical axis.
materials: Blank paper for unmarked number lines

periods.activity_title: Number Line Practice and Meeting the Token Model

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 10.1 p.253
textbook_items_in_class.description: Mark 3 positive and 3 negative numbers on a given number line (–10 to +10).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 10.1 p.254
textbook_items_in_class.description: Is 2 > –3? Why? Is –2 < 3? Why? Justify using the number line.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 10.1 p.254
textbook_items_in_class.description: Compute six integer expressions: –5+0, 7+(–7), –10+20, 10–20, 7–(–7), –8–(–10).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example (Token addition +5 and –8), p.256
textbook_items_in_class.description: Lay out 5 positive and 8 negative tokens; remove 5 zero pairs; 3 negative tokens remain. (+5)+(–8)=–3.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 10.2 p.257
textbook_items_in_class.description: Complete four additions using token diagrams: (+6)+(+4), (–3)+(–2), (+5)+(–7), (–2)+(+6).

time_bands.activity: Students complete Figure it Out Q1, section 10.1 p.253 ("Mark 3 positive and 3 negative numbers on a given number line...."), Figure it Out Q3, section 10.1 p.254 ("Is 2 > –3? Why? Is –2 < 3? Why?...."), and Figure it Out Q4, section 10.1 p.254 ("Compute six integer expressions: –5+0, 7+(–7), –10+20....") — consolidating the horizontal number line and the computation rules from the building.

Teacher introduces the token model with Example (Token addition +5 and –8), p.256 ("Lay out 5 positive and 8 negative tokens; remove 5 zero pairs; 3 negative tokens remain....") — students physically represent tokens using two-coloured counters or hand-drawn circles (+ and –) before cancelling pairs.
Students work on Figure it Out Q1, section 10.2 p.257 ("Complete four additions using token diagrams....") — drawing token sets, crossing out zero pairs, and writing the addition statement for each.

Students compare the token answer for (+5)+(–7) with the building answer obtained by the same calculation, confirming that both models yield the same result and discussing why the zero-pair idea matches the additive inverse concept.

periods.teacher_notes: Having worked fluently with the building and number line, students now meet a second concrete model for the same arithmetic. The connection to note: cancelling a zero pair in tokens is exactly the additive inverse idea already seen in the building. Watch for students who count total tokens rather than cancelling pairs first — insist on the crossing-out step before reading the remainder.
materials: Two-coloured counters or blank paper for drawing token circles

periods.activity_title: Subtraction with Tokens: Adding Zero Pairs to Take Away

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example (Token subtraction +5 minus +4), p.257
textbook_items_in_class.description: From 5 positives, remove 4; 1 positive remains. (+5)–(+4)=+1.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example (Token subtraction –7 minus –5), p.257
textbook_items_in_class.description: From 7 negatives, remove 5; 2 negatives remain. (–7)–(–5)=–2. Also prompts: is this the same as (–7)+(+5)?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example (Token subtraction +5 minus +6), p.257-258
textbook_items_in_class.description: 5 positives, need to remove 6 — not enough. Add one zero pair; now remove 6 positives; 1 negative left. (+5)–(+6)=–1.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example (Token subtraction +4 minus –6), p.258
textbook_items_in_class.description: 4 positives, need to remove 6 negatives — none present. Add 6 zero pairs (6 positives + 6 negatives); remove 6 negatives; 10 positives remain. +4–(–6)=+10.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 10.2 p.258
Figure it Out Q1, section 10.2 p.259
textbook_items_in_class.description: Subtract –3–(+5) using tokens. How many zero pairs are needed? What is the result?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 10.2 p.259

time_bands.activity: Teacher demonstrates Example (Token subtraction +5 minus +4), p.257 ("From 5 positives, remove 4; 1 positive remains...."), Example (Token subtraction –7 minus –5), p.257 ("From 7 negatives, remove 5; 2 negatives remain...."), Example (Token subtraction +5 minus +6), p.257-258 ("5 positives, need to remove 6 — add one zero pair...."), and Example (Token subtraction +4 minus –6), p.258 ("4 positives, need to remove 6 negatives — add 6 zero pairs....") — using drawn token circles on the board, asking students to direct each step.

Students work on Figure it Out Q1, section 10.2 p.258 ("Evaluate six differences using tokens....") — drawing full token diagrams, marking which pairs to add when needed, crossing out removed tokens, and recording the result.

Students tackle Figure it Out Q1, section 10.2 p.259 ("Subtract –3–(+5) using tokens. How many zero pairs are needed?....") and Figure it Out Q2, section 10.2 p.259 ("Evaluate six expressions using tokens....") — working in pairs so that one draws tokens while the other verifies by checking with the building/number-line method.

Whole-class debrief: teacher writes (+4)–(–6) and its token solution alongside the number-line/conversion solution, asking 'Do both give +10?' — students confirm and articulate in their own words why subtracting a negative is the same as adding a positive.

periods.teacher_notes: The zero-pair insertion step is the conceptual heart of token subtraction: students who skip adding the pairs and guess the answer will lose the model's explanatory power. A frequent error is adding only one zero pair when multiple are needed — prompt students to count how many tokens of the required type are missing before deciding how many pairs to add. Example (Token subtraction +4 minus –6), p.258 is a strong self-study reference for students who wish to revisit the hardest case.
materials: Two-coloured counters or paper for drawn token circles
Pencils and erasers for crossing out tokens

periods.activity_title: Token Practice Wrap-up and Integers in Banking

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 10.2 p.257
textbook_items_in_class.description: Cancel zero pairs in two given token sets (a: 3 positive + 5 negative; b: 6 positive + 3 negative). State which floor the attendant is on and write the corresponding addition statement.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 10.2 p.258
Figure it Out Q1, section 10.3 p.260
textbook_items_in_class.description: Bank account: start at ₹0, add credits of ₹30, ₹40, ₹50 and debits of ₹40, ₹50, ₹60. What is the balance?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 10.3 p.260
textbook_items_in_class.description: Bank account: start at ₹0, debits of ₹1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128 and a single credit of ₹256. What is the balance?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 10.3 p.260
textbook_items_in_class.description: Why is it generally better to keep a positive bank balance? When might a temporary negative balance be worthwhile?

time_bands.activity: Students complete Figure it Out Q2, section 10.2 p.257 ("Cancel zero pairs in two given token sets....") and Figure it Out Q2, section 10.2 p.258 ("Complete six subtractions....") — a quick consolidation of the token method before the context shifts.

Teacher introduces the banking context from section 10.3: credits are positive changes, debits are negative changes, and a negative balance means the account is overdrawn. Students solve Figure it Out Q1, section 10.3 p.260 ("Bank account: start at ₹0, add credits of ₹30, ₹40, ₹50 and debits of ₹40, ₹50, ₹60....") by listing each transaction as a signed integer and summing.

Students solve Figure it Out Q2, section 10.3 p.260 ("Bank account: debits of ₹1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128 and a credit of ₹256....") — recognising the doubling pattern to find the total debit before comparing with the credit.

Class discusses Figure it Out Q3, section 10.3 p.260 ("Why is it generally better to keep a positive bank balance? When might a temporary negative balance be worthwhile?....") — students share reasoning in pairs, then one response is collected from the class and written on the board as a model answer.

periods.teacher_notes: The transition from abstract token diagrams to a real financial context anchors integer arithmetic in a situation students can reason about socially as well as mathematically. Watch for students who add all numbers without regard to sign — emphasise that each debit must be recorded as a negative integer before summing. Figure it Out Q2 p.260 is a valuable extension for quick finishers, as the doubling pattern is a pleasing numerical discovery.
materials: Blank paper for listing transactions in a column

periods.activity_title: Heights, Depths, and Temperatures: Integers Everywhere

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 10.3 p.261
textbook_items_in_class.description: Read heights A–G from a geographical cross-section chart and fill in the values.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 10.3 p.261
textbook_items_in_class.description: Identify the highest and lowest points in the geographical cross-section.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 10.3 p.261
textbook_items_in_class.description: Write points A–G in decreasing and increasing order of heights.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 10.3 p.261
textbook_items_in_class.description: What is the highest point above sea level on Earth and its height?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 10.3 p.261
textbook_items_in_class.description: What is the lowest point on Earth with respect to sea level? What is its (negative) height?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 10.3 p.262
textbook_items_in_class.description: Research and find places in India where temperatures go below 0°C. What do they have in common and why?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 10.3 p.262
textbook_items_in_class.description: Match four temperatures (14°C, 8°C, –2°C, –4°C) with four times of day in Leh, Ladakh in November.

time_bands.activity: Students read the geographical cross-section diagram and complete Figure it Out Q1, section 10.3 p.261 ("Read heights A–G and fill in the values...."), Figure it Out Q2, section 10.3 p.261 ("Identify the highest and lowest points...."), and Figure it Out Q3, section 10.3 p.261 ("Write points A–G in decreasing and increasing order....") — ordering the signed heights on a horizontal number line drawn in their notebooks.

Students research Figure it Out Q4, section 10.3 p.261 ("What is the highest point above sea level on Earth and its height?....") and Figure it Out Q5, section 10.3 p.261 ("What is the lowest point on Earth with respect to sea level?....") — using the textbook's cross-section as a reference scale and recording both values as signed integers.

Teacher introduces the temperature context: 0°C is the freezing point of water, sub-zero temperatures are negative integers. Students discuss Figure it Out Q1, section 10.3 p.262 ("Research places in India where temperatures go below 0°C....") in pairs, pooling geographical knowledge, and then solve Figure it Out Q2, section 10.3 p.262 ("Match four temperatures with four times of day in Leh, Ladakh in November....")
Brief class share: students explain their temperature matches and justify using the ordering of integers, connecting the warmest temperature to midday and the coldest to early morning.

periods.teacher_notes: Having applied integers to banking, this unit moves to geography and temperature — contexts where the zero reference point (sea level, freezing point) is physically meaningful and motivates the sign convention. A common slip is ordering heights by their absolute values rather than their signed values, placing –300 m above –50 m; returning to the cross-section diagram resolves this. Figure it Out Q1 p.262 is an opportunity for students to bring in knowledge from their science and geography lessons.
materials: Atlas or geographical reference if available

periods.activity_title: Border Sums: Filling Integer Grids and Finding Patterns

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 10.4 p.263
textbook_items_in_class.description: Compute the four border sums (top row, bottom row, left column, right column) for the second hollow integer grid and identify the border sum.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 10.4 p.264
textbook_items_in_class.description: Complete three hollow integer grids to achieve specified border sums: +4, –2, –4.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 10.4 p.264
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find more than one way to fill the border-sum –4 grid.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 10.4 p.264
textbook_items_in_class.description: Which grids can be filled in multiple ways? What could be the reason?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 10.4 p.264
textbook_items_in_class.description: Make a border integer square puzzle and challenge classmates.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the hollow integer grid from section 10.4: the border cells (top row, bottom row, left column, right column) must all sum to the same border sum. Students read the two example grids from the textbook (border sums 0 and –3) and verify by summing each border independently.

Students solve Figure it Out Q1, section 10.4 p.263 ("Compute the four border sums for the second hollow integer grid and identify the border sum....") — writing out each sum explicitly and checking consistency.

Students attempt Figure it Out Q2, section 10.4 p.264 ("Complete three hollow integer grids for border sums +4, –2, –4....") and Figure it Out Q3, section 10.4 p.264 ("Find more than one way to fill the border-sum –4 grid....") — working in small groups, comparing their fillings, and noting whether different groups found different valid answers.

Groups discuss Figure it Out Q4, section 10.4 p.264 ("Which grids can be filled in multiple ways? What could be the reason?....") — students articulate their reasoning in writing before sharing, then volunteers present their arguments to the class.
Students begin Figure it Out Q5, section 10.4 p.264 ("Make a border integer square puzzle and challenge classmates....") — designing one grid each to be exchanged and solved by a partner.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit asks students to reason about why certain grids have unique solutions while others admit multiple — the key insight is that when the corner cells are shared by two borders, changing one corner propagates a constraint. Encourage students to state their reasoning in a full sentence ('This grid has multiple solutions because…') rather than just showing another filling. Watch for students who adjust a single cell without re-checking all four border sums.
materials: Grid paper for drawing and filling hollow squares

periods.activity_title: Amazing Grids, Dice Sums, and Integer Sequences

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 10.4 p.265
textbook_items_in_class.description: In the amazing grid, try the circle-and-strike game afresh with different chosen numbers. Does the final sum change?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 10.4 p.265
textbook_items_in_class.description: Play the circle-and-strike game on two other provided 4×4 grids (arithmetic progression grids).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 10.4 p.265
textbook_items_in_class.description: What is special about these grids — is the 'magic' in the numbers, the arrangement, or both? Can you make more such grids?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 10.4 p.265
textbook_items_in_class.description: Two dice with faces –1, 2, –3, 4, –5, 6. Find the numbers between –10 and +12 that cannot be obtained as a sum of the two dice.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 10.4 p.265
textbook_items_in_class.description: Solve eight integer arithmetic expressions arranged in a 2×4 table: 8–13, (–8)–(13), (–13)–(–8), (–13)+(–8), 8+(–13), (–8)–(–13), (13)–8, 13–(–8).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q6, section 10.4 p.266

time_bands.activity: Students play the circle-and-strike game with Figure it Out Q1, section 10.4 p.265 ("Try the circle-and-strike game afresh with different chosen numbers. Does the final sum change?....") and Figure it Out Q2, section 10.4 p.265 ("Play the game on two other 4×4 grids....") — each student records their four circled numbers and the sum, then compares with classmates to observe the invariance.

Class discusses Figure it Out Q3, section 10.4 p.265 ("What is special about these grids — is the magic in the numbers, the arrangement, or both?....") — students propose and debate conjectures, with teacher recording different explanations on the board without adjudicating immediately.

Students work on Figure it Out Q3, section 10.4 p.265 ("Two dice with faces –1, 2, –3, 4, –5, 6. Find numbers between –10 and +12 that cannot be a sum....") — systematically listing possible sums and identifying gaps, using a table to organise their work.

Students solve Figure it Out Q4, section 10.4 p.265 ("Solve eight integer arithmetic expressions in the table....") — working individually, then checking in pairs, and Figure it Out Q6, section 10.4 p.266 ("Complete three integer sequences....") — identifying the rule before filling each blank.
Quick share: teacher asks one student to explain the rule for sequence (b) and another for sequence (c), reinforcing that a sequence pattern can mix alternating operations.

periods.teacher_notes: The amazing grid's invariant sum is the conceptual peak of this unit: students who reason about why the sum is fixed (each row-value and column-value is selected exactly once) encounter a genuine mathematical insight. Avoid confirming the explanation immediately — let the class argue it out. Watch for students who evaluate (–8)–(–13) as –21 by treating both negatives as making the result more negative.
materials: Grid paper for the amazing-grid game

time_bands.activity: Students complete Figure it Out Q1, section 10.4 p.265 ("Write all integers between four given pairs in increasing order....") and Figure it Out Q2, section 10.4 p.265 ("Give three integers whose sum is –8....") — the latter inviting multiple valid answers, with teacher noting several on the board to show the variety.

Students work on Figure it Out Q5, section 10.4 p.265-266 ("Find three historical years....") — drawing a number line that includes both BCE and CE years, accounting for the absence of a year 0, and expressing each answer as a signed integer.

Students attempt Figure it Out Q7, section 10.4 p.266 ("From six integer cards, construct an expression whose value is closest to –30....") — working in pairs to trial different combinations systematically, recording each attempt and comparing results.

Students reason through Figure it Out Q8, section 10.4 p.266 ("Determine whether each combination type is always positive, always negative, or can be either....") — providing one example and one counter-example for each 'can be either' case, and a clear argument for the deterministic cases. Students then tackle Figure it Out Q9, section 10.4 p.266 ("A string of 100 tokens in a repeating pattern (+++––)....") by finding how many complete cycles fit and the value of each cycle.

Quick class check of the token-string answer: students explain how many cycles of five fit in 100 tokens and what the running sum is, connecting the repeating pattern to the additive structure of integers.

periods.teacher_notes: The historical year problem is a rich site of confusion: students often forget that BCE years count backwards and that there is no year 0, so 1 BCE is followed immediately by 1 CE. Insist that students draw the timeline before writing an expression. For Figure it Out Q8, the sign-reasoning task, encourage students to write out two concrete examples before making a general claim — this inductive habit of mind is central to the chapter's spirit.
materials: Blank paper for number line timeline

periods.activity_title: Brahmagupta's Rules: History Meets the Number Line

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 10.5 p.268

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 10.5 p.268
textbook_items_in_class.description: Give your own examples of each of Brahmagupta's rules for addition and subtraction.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the historical arc of section 10.5: Chinese rods (Nine Chapters, c. 1st–2nd century CE), Kautilya's recognition of negative balances (c. 300 BCE), the Bakśhālī symbol for negatives, and Brahmagupta's Brāhma-sphuṭa-siddhānta (628 CE) as the first complete explicit rules for integer arithmetic — students listen and take notes on the names and approximate dates, connecting them to the token-model and number-line work they have already done.

Students read Brahmagupta's ten rules (five for addition, five for subtraction) from the textbook and complete Figure it Out Q1, section 10.5 p.268 ("Explain each of Brahmagupta's rules in terms of Bela's Building of Fun or the number line....") — writing one sentence of explanation and one building/number-line diagram for each rule.

Students work on Figure it Out Q2, section 10.5 p.268 ("Give your own examples of each of Brahmagupta's rules....") — choosing their own integers, computing the result using the rule, and verifying using the number line or token method.

Whole-class discussion: teacher asks 'Why did European mathematicians resist negative numbers for so long?' — students respond using what the section says about Lazare Carnot and the 18th century, connecting historical resistance to their own initial instincts when first encountering floors below zero.

periods.teacher_notes: Brahmagupta's rule 'the sum of two negatives is negative' and 'subtracting a negative is adding a positive' are exactly what students have demonstrated through the building, tokens, and number line — the historical framing rewards all that prior work by naming it as a genuine mathematical achievement. Watch for students who copy the rules without translating them: insist that every rule has an accompanying building or number-line sketch. Figure it Out Q2 p.268 is an excellent self-study item for revisiting any rule that felt unclear.
materials: Blank paper for diagrams alongside each rule

items.prompt: In Bela's Building of Fun, Floor 0 is the ground floor, floors above ground are positive, and floors below ground are negative. The Toy Store is on Floor –1 and the Cinema is on Floor –3. Which statement correctly describes the relationship between these two floors?

options.label: A
options.text: Floor –1 and Floor –3 are at the same height because both are negative.

options.label: B
options.text: Floor –1 is higher than Floor –3 because –1 is greater than –3.

options.label: C
options.text: Floor –3 is higher than Floor –1 because 3 is greater than 1.

options.label: D
options.text: Floor –3 is higher than Floor –1 because negative numbers increase as they move away from zero.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Floor –1 is higher than Floor –3 because –1 is greater than –3. On the integer number line (or the building's vertical axis), numbers increase as you move upward, so –1 lies above –3.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the vertical ordering of integers: a less negative number corresponds to a higher floor, so –1 > –3.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student compares absolute values (3 > 1) and incorrectly assigns that larger absolute value to a higher position, ignoring the negative sign.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student treats all negative numbers as equivalent in position, not recognising that negative integers have a definite order.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has a misconception that numbers 'increase' in magnitude as they move further from zero in the negative direction, confusing magnitude with value.

inclusivity.support: Let the student sketch the building and mark Floor –1 and Floor –3 before choosing.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to write a general rule about which of two negative floors is always higher.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 10.1 p.245
exercise.description: Start from Floor +2 and press –3. Where do you reach? Write an expression.

items.prompt: A lift in Bela's Building starts at Floor +4. The passenger presses +1 and then presses –3. Which expression gives the floor the passenger reaches, and what is that floor?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: (+4) + (+1) + (–3) = +2. The passenger starts at +4, moves up 1 floor to +5, then moves down 3 floors to +2.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the rule Starting Floor + Movement = Target Floor for each button press in sequence, or combine all movements: +1 + (–3) = –2, then +4 + (–2) = +2.

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student added all the digits 4 + 1 + 3 = 8 and then applied a negative sign without following the signed-arithmetic rule.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student added all three numbers as if they were all positive: 4 + 1 + 3 = 8, ignoring the negative sign on –3.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student may have paired +1 and –3 incorrectly, perhaps computing –3 + (+1) = –2 then +4 + (–4) = 0 by a sign error.

inclusivity.support: Let the student trace each button press one at a time on a sketch of the building before combining.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to write a different sequence of button presses that also lands on Floor +2 from Floor +4.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 10.1 p.245
exercise.description: Evaluate seven expressions (a–g) as Starting Floor + Movement: (+1)+(+4), (+4)+(+1), (+4)+(–3), (–1)+(+2), (–1)+(+1), 0+(+2), 0+(–2).

items.prompt: Six floors are listed: +3, –1, 0, –4, +2, –6. Which of the following arranges these floors in increasing order (lowest floor first)?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: –6, –4, –1, 0, +2, +3. Floors further below ground have smaller integer values, so –6 < –4 < –1 < 0 < +2 < +3.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Place each floor on the vertical number line; the lowest physical floor corresponds to the smallest integer, so read from most negative to most positive.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student ordered by absolute value in decreasing order, confusing 'higher floor' with 'larger number' and reversing the sequence.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student grouped negatives by absolute value incorrectly, placing –1 before –4 instead of after, suggesting the student ordered negatives by digit size without the sign.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student placed 0 first and then ordered negatives as if positive, suggesting confusion about where zero sits relative to negative numbers.

inclusivity.support: Let the student draw a vertical line and physically place each floor before choosing the order.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to add two more floors of their own choice and insert them in the correct positions.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 10.1 p.247
exercise.description: Compare six pairs of integers using < or > by referring to the Building of Fun: –2 vs +5, –5 vs +4, –5 vs –3, +6 vs –6, 0 vs –4, 0 vs +4.

items.prompt: Brahmagupta stated a rule (c. 628 CE) for adding two negative numbers. State this rule in your own words and give one example using integers to illustrate it.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: When two negative numbers are added, the result is negative and its size equals the sum of their sizes. For example, (–5) + (–3) = –8: the sum of the sizes is 5 + 3 = 8 and the result is negative.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Recall Brahmagupta's rule: the sum of two negatives is negative, with magnitude equal to the sum of the two magnitudes.

inclusivity.support: Let the student look back at the section's quoted rules and identify the one that describes two negatives before writing their explanation.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to give a second example and explain the same rule using movement on the number line.

exercise.description: Explain each of Brahmagupta's rules for addition and subtraction in terms of Bela's Building of Fun or the number line.

items.prompt: A hollow integer grid is a 3×3 grid where only the eight border cells are filled. The border sum is the common total of the top row, bottom row, left column, and right column. Riya fills the top-left cell with –5 and the top-right cell with +3. She says: 'If I want the top-row border sum to be –4, the top-middle cell must be –2.' Is Riya correct? Justify your answer.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Riya is correct. The top row has three cells: –5, top-middle, and +3. Their sum must be –4. Setting up the equation: (–5) + top-middle + (+3) = –4, which simplifies to top-middle + (–2) = –4, so top-middle = –2. Check: (–5) + (–2) + (+3) = –4. ✓
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Write the border-sum equation for the top row, substitute the known values, and solve for the missing cell by integer arithmetic.

inclusivity.support: Suggest the student write out the equation (–5) + ? + (+3) = –4 and solve for ? step by step using the number line.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to find a different set of three integers (not involving –5 or +3) that also gives a top-row sum of –4.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 10.4 p.263
exercise.description: Compute the four border sums (top row, bottom row, left column, right column) for the second hollow integer grid and identify the border sum.

items.prompt: In the amazing grid activity, a student plays the circle-and-strike game twice on the same 4×4 grid and gets the same final sum both times, even though she circled completely different numbers each time. Her classmate says this must be a coincidence. Explain, using the structure of the game, why the sum is always the same regardless of which numbers are circled.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: In the circle-and-strike game, you circle one number in an uncrossed row and column each turn, crossing out the rest of that row and column. After four turns, exactly one number from each row and one from each column has been circled. Because every row contains one entry from each column, and the grid's values are built so that the total of one-per-row-one-per-column selections is fixed, the sum cannot change. Concretely: each row contributes one number and each column contributes one number, and the grid is arranged so that every such selection produces the same total. It is not a coincidence — the invariance is built into the structure of the grid.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: The game forces exactly one selection per row and one per column; the grid is structured so that every such selection yields the same total sum.

inclusivity.support: Suggest the student try two specific different selections on the same small grid and check both sums before writing the explanation.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to alter one number in the grid and determine whether the invariance still holds, and what it would take to preserve it.

items.prompt: Arjun says: 'The integers strictly between –8 and –15 are –9, –10, –11, –12, –13, and –14.' Priya says: 'You have them in the wrong order — they should go from –14 down to –9.' Who is right, and what is the correct increasing order of all integers strictly between –8 and –15?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Arjun identified the correct set of integers (–9, –10, –11, –12, –13, –14) but Priya is right that the order Arjun listed is decreasing, not increasing. The correct increasing order is: –14, –13, –12, –11, –10, –9. On the number line, –14 is furthest to the left (smallest) and –9 is closest to zero (largest among these).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Place the integers on a number line; increasing order runs left to right, so –14 < –13 < –12 < –11 < –10 < –9.

inclusivity.support: Suggest the student draw a short number line, mark –15 and –8, and list the integers between them from left to right.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to explain in one sentence why –14 is less than –9, even though 14 > 9.

items.prompt: A lift starts at Floor –3. The passenger presses –2 (going down). What floor does the lift reach? Write the addition expression and find the answer. Then state what button the passenger must press from the new floor to return directly to Floor 0.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The lift starts at –3 and moves down 2 floors: (–3) + (–2) = –5. The lift reaches Floor –5. To return from Floor –5 to Floor 0, the passenger presses +5, because (–5) + (+5) = 0.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply Starting Floor + Movement = Target Floor for the downward press, then use the additive inverse (+5) to return to 0 from –5.

inclusivity.support: Let the student sketch the building and count floors down from –3 before writing the expression.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to find two other multi-step button presses that also start at –5 and end at Floor 0.

exercise.description: Complete ten subtraction expressions (a–j) as movement from Starting Floor to Target Floor: (+1)–(+4), 0–(+2), (+4)–(+1), 0–(–2), (+4)–(–3), (–4)–(–3), (–1)–(+2), (–2)–(–2), (–1)–(+1), (+3)–(–3).

items.prompt: A mine shaft has its surface at level 0. A worker is at level –50 m. She needs to reach level +200 m. Write and evaluate the subtraction expression that gives the distance she must travel. Then confirm your answer by writing the equivalent addition expression.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Distance needed = Target – Starting = (+200) – (–50) = +250. Subtraction of a negative equals addition of the positive: (+200) – (–50) = (+200) + (+50) = +250. The worker must travel +250 m upward. Check: (–50) + (+250) = +200. ✓
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use Target Floor – Starting Floor = Movement, then convert subtraction of a negative to addition of the positive: (+200)–(–50) = (+200)+(+50) = +250.

inclusivity.support: Let the student draw a vertical number line, mark –50 and +200, and count the gap before writing the expression.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to write a mine problem of their own with a different starting level and verify it using the same two-form approach.

exercise.description: Complete seven expressions using the mine/larger number context (a–g): (+40)+__=+200, (+40)+__=–200, (–50)+__=+200, (–50)+__=–200, (–200)–(–40), (+200)–(+40), (–200)–(+40). Verify using the mineshaft.

items.prompt: Mark the integers –7, –2, 0, +5 on a number line drawn from –10 to +10. Then compute: (–7) + (+5). Show your working using the number line (describe the starting point and the movement).

teacher_guide.expected_answer: On the number line, start at –7 and move +5 units to the right: (–7) + (+5) = –2. The landing point is –2, which is one of the marked integers on the line.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Start at –7 on the number line, move 5 steps to the right (positive direction), and land at –2.

inclusivity.support: Let the student draw the number line, mark –7, and physically count 5 steps to the right before writing the answer.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to identify a second pair of marked integers whose sum can be read directly from the number line and compute it.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 10.1 p.253
exercise.description: Mark 3 positive and 3 negative numbers on a given number line (–10 to +10).

items.prompt: Use the token model to evaluate (–6) – (–9). Show: (a) the tokens you start with, (b) how many zero pairs you need to add and why, (c) which tokens you remove, and (d) the result.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: (a) Start with 6 negative tokens. (b) We need to remove 9 negative tokens but only have 6, so we are 3 short — add 3 zero pairs (3 positive + 3 negative tokens), giving 9 negative tokens and 3 positive tokens. (c) Remove all 9 negative tokens. (d) 3 positive tokens remain, so (–6) – (–9) = +3. Verify: (–6) + (+9) = +3. ✓
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Lay out 6 negative tokens; add 3 zero pairs to create enough negatives to remove; remove 9 negatives; read the remaining 3 positive tokens.

inclusivity.support: Let the student draw circles labelled + and – on paper and physically cross out tokens as they remove them.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to verify the token result using the equivalent addition (–6) + (+9) and explain why the two methods must agree.

items.prompt: A lift attendant collects tokens throughout his shift. At the end, he has 6 positive tokens and 3 negative tokens in his pocket. Cancel all zero pairs and determine which floor he is on. Write the addition statement that represents his token collection.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 6 positive + 3 negative: cancel 3 zero pairs, leaving 3 positive tokens. The attendant is on Floor +3. Addition statement: (+6) + (–3) = +3.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Cancel one positive with one negative to form each zero pair; the 3 remaining positive tokens give Floor +3.

inclusivity.support: Let the student draw 6 plus signs and 3 minus signs, then draw lines connecting pairs before counting the remainder.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to find a different combination of positive and negative tokens that also leaves the attendant on Floor +3.

items.prompt: Meera's bank account starts at ₹0. She receives credits of ₹45 and ₹30, and makes debits of ₹20, ₹60, and ₹15. Write each transaction as a signed integer, find the final balance, and state whether her account is in credit or overdrawn.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Credits: +45, +30. Debits: –20, –60, –15. Sum: 0 + 45 + 30 + (–20) + (–60) + (–15) = 75 + (–95) = –20. Final balance = –₹20. The account is overdrawn (negative balance).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add all credits as positive integers and all debits as negative integers; the sum is the final balance, and a negative result means the account is overdrawn.

inclusivity.support: Let the student list each transaction in a column — credits with a + sign and debits with a – sign — then sum the positives and negatives separately before combining.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to find the single minimum credit that would bring the balance back to exactly ₹0.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 10.3 p.260
exercise.description: Bank account: start at ₹0, add credits of ₹30, ₹40, ₹50 and debits of ₹40, ₹50, ₹60. What is the balance?
